title: 📊 CFO Chair: Your First Quarterly Close
subtitle: Manage cash, board, audit, and the analyst call — in one quarter
theme: First-time CFO at a Series-D fintech navigating quarter-end, audit, and forecast variance
description: You just took the CFO seat at Vela, a Series-D B2B fintech ($85M ARR, 14-month runway, considering an IPO in 18 months). Your first quarterly close is in 60 days, you have a board meeting at week 4, an audit walkthrough at week 6, and a debt covenant test at quarter-end. Every choice ripples through P&L, cash, runway, board confidence, and audit risk.
learning_objectives: Close a quarter on time without surprises — variance analysis, accruals, cutoffs
Communicate forecast misses to the board: own it, explain it, fix it
Manage 13-week cash + working capital under debt covenants
Distinguish operating vs board-level decisions; prep audit committee correctly
Build calibrated revenue forecasts the CEO and board can act on

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Each round is one week of the quarter. Read your P&L, cash, and runway before deciding.
Author your Q4 OKRs and a BCG matrix of business segments when prompted — both LLM-graded.
Survive the audit walkthrough, hit the covenant test, and own the analyst call narrative.
tips: Always answer the board's actual question — not the question you wanted them to ask.
Auditors don't kill companies; surprises kill auditor relationships.
Cash is a fact; revenue is an opinion. Reconcile early.

target_audience: First-time CFOs, finance leaders, MBA finance students

psychological_framework.description: CFO dimensions: commercial acumen, governance judgment, controllership, cash discipline, decision quality, communication.

core_skills.name: Commercial Acumen
core_skills.description: Reading P&L, unit economics, pricing as a coherent story.

core_skills.name: Governance Judgment
core_skills.description: Board prep, audit committee, separation of operating vs board-level.

core_skills.name: Controllership
core_skills.description: Close discipline, accruals, controls, audit readiness.

core_skills.name: Decision Quality
core_skills.description: Calibrated forecasts; reversibility; pre-mortems on numbers.

core_skills.name: Executive Communication
core_skills.description: Owning the narrative on misses; analyst-call discipline.

llm_config.audience_default: First-time CFO of a $85M ARR Series-D fintech

hallmarks: Owns misses early — never spins to the board on slide 1
Restates correctly when auditors are right
Presents BCG segments honestly — calls Question Marks by name
Defaults to 'wait and see' when data is uncomfortable
Defends positions against auditors that they can't win
Hides bad news in slide 14 instead of leading with it
Treats covenant cure period as something to negotiate around

rounds.title: Week 1 — Landing in the Seat
rounds.scenario: Day 3 in the chair. The Controller hands you a draft P&L variance: revenue is tracking 6% below plan with 60 days left in the quarter. Two board members already emailed asking 'are we on plan?'
rounds.ai_image_prompt: New CFO at desk on first week, financial statements open, two monitors with dashboards

choices.label: Run a 48-hour re-forecast with sales leadership; send a written update to the board Friday
choices.feedback: You owned the narrative early. Board respected the speed; CEO trusted you faster.

decision_record.rationale: Speed of honest signal beats polished delay

choices.expert_rationale: First close = trust-building. A 48-hour written re-forecast with sales beats silence: it shows control of the data and writing-culture discipline. Boards forgive misses; they don't forgive surprises.

choices.label: Wait — pipeline can swing back; respond to board email with 'on plan, will update at QBR'
choices.feedback: Pipeline didn't swing. Board email at QBR landed badly. You started behind.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Silence in week 1 is read as 'not on top of the numbers.' By the time the board emails you, you've lost the framing fight.

choices.label: Tell the board this gap is inherited — 'plan was set before I arrived'
choices.feedback: Defensive. You lost trust before you earned it. Audit chair flagged you.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Blaming inherited plans is a tell that you don't yet own the seat. The board hired you to fix it, not narrate it.

rounds.title: Week 2 — Finance Function OKRs
rounds.scenario: The CEO asked for your function's Q4 OKRs by Friday so she can align cross-functional plans. Submit them now — the steering committee will use them to grade you.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Finance team in glass meeting room reviewing OKR slides

choices.label: Submit 3 objectives × 3 KRs (close in 12d, audit-zero-surprises, 13-wk cash variance ≤5%)
choices.feedback: Tight, measurable, owned. CEO forwarded them as a template to peer functions.
choices.expert_rationale: 3 objectives × 3 KRs forces prioritization (close-on-time, audit-clean, cash-discipline). Vague OKRs let everyone hide.

choices.label: Submit 5 objectives × 4 KRs each (broad coverage)
choices.feedback: Too many priorities = no priorities. CEO kicked it back.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: 5×4 OKRs is 20 KRs — nobody owns 20 things. Vague OKRs are the #1 reason finance functions miss audit deadlines.

choices.label: Push OKRs by 2 weeks — 'still understanding the org'
choices.feedback: Delay is the wrong tax. CEO assigned you a deadline-watcher.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: 'Still understanding the org' is a quarter you'll never get back. By Q2 you're already behind.

rounds.title: Week 4 — The Board Meeting
rounds.scenario: Quarterly board meeting Thursday. The CEO wants you to present the cash plan, IPO-readiness gap, and a recommended response to the revenue miss. Audit chair Jamal will press you on controls.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Boardroom at golden hour, CFO presenting on screen, directors watching

choices.label: Own the miss in slide 1; present a 3-lever recovery plan with 60-70% confidence
choices.feedback: Lead investor leaned in; audit chair quietly told CEO this CFO 'gets it'.

decision_record.rationale: Owning misses is the only durable pattern with this board

choices.expert_rationale: Slide 1 = own the miss + 3-lever recovery at 60-70% confidence (calibrated). This is the move that gets you re-hired by your board chair next quarter.

choices.label: Open with NRR 118% and YoY ARR growth; bury the miss on slide 14
choices.feedback: Lead investor saw it for what it was. Audit chair scheduled a 1:1 'about controls'.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Burying the miss on slide 14 means the audit chair finds it. Once trust is broken, every future variance is interpreted in the worst light.

choices.label: Ask the board for an extra 4 weeks before recommitting to a Q4 number
choices.feedback: Board granted it but Q3 plan now drifts. CEO needs a number to give sales.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Asking for more time is the right move at week 4 only if you've already shown a recovery thesis. Cold ask = panic signal.

inbox_events.subject: Found a tagging error in revenue ledger
inbox_events.body: We classified $180K of services revenue as product. CFO call: do I patch quietly or escalate to audit committee?

choices.label: Escalate to audit committee — disclose now
Patch quietly — fix internally before close

rounds.title: Week 6 — Audit Walkthrough
rounds.scenario: Big-4 audit team is on-site. They flagged a revenue-recognition issue: a $4M deal closed in Q2 was booked under ASC 606 with a single performance obligation, but the deal has separate professional-services and SaaS components. The Controller wants to defend the existing treatment.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Audit team and controller at conference room table reviewing contracts

choices.label: Restate to two performance obligations, take the prior-period adjustment, walk audit committee through it
choices.feedback: Audit chair commended the call. You took a 1.2% Q2 revenue haircut but bought 4 quarters of credibility.

forecast_prompt.question: Forecast Q3 audit findings dollar impact (USD). Provide an 80% confidence interval — narrower interval earns more credit if your true value is covered.

choices.expert_rationale: Two performance obligations under ASC 606 isn't negotiable when the auditors are right. Take the prior-period adjustment, walk the audit committee through it, ship the close.

choices.label: Defend the existing single-obligation treatment with Controller; ask audit team for a memo
choices.feedback: Audit team escalated to their national office; opinion now in question. Audit chair worried.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Defending a position the auditors will eventually win burns credibility you'll need next quarter. Pick your audit fights — this isn't one.

choices.label: Negotiate with auditors: agree to a future-period change, no restatement
choices.feedback: Auditors pushed back hard. They want either restatement or a qualified opinion. You burned a week.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A 'future-period change, no restatement' deal is what controllers do when they don't want to escalate. Auditors remember; the next surprise is bigger.

rounds.title: Week 8 — Covenant Test
rounds.scenario: End-of-quarter covenant test on a $30M revolver: minimum unrestricted cash $25M, max 6-mo trailing burn $20M. Current cash $26M, trailing burn $19.8M. A pending vendor payment of $1.2M falls due Tuesday. Treasury asks: pay or delay?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Cash management dashboard with covenant gauges, ledger entries

choices.label: Delay the vendor payment 7 days, communicate proactively, hold cash above $25M
choices.feedback: Vendor was annoyed but understood. You preserved the covenant and avoided a cure period.
choices.expert_rationale: Vendor delay + proactive communication preserves cash, protects the covenant, and demonstrates the cash-discipline muscle the board hired you for. Cure periods aren't free — banks downgrade you internally even if they don't act.

choices.label: Pay the vendor on time; breach the covenant by $200K; trigger cure period
choices.feedback: Lender called. You're in technical default. Cure cost: $80K + reputational cost.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Breaching the covenant by $200K to pay a vendor on time is the textbook bad trade. You save a vendor relationship and burn a banking one.

choices.label: Draw $5M on the revolver to create headroom; pay vendor on time
choices.feedback: Headroom secured but interest cost increases burn rate. Audit chair asked why.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Drawing the revolver to avoid a 7-day vendor delay is expensive optionality. Cash discipline = use the levers in order; revolver is last, not first.

rounds.title: Week 12 — Close + Analyst Call Prep
rounds.scenario: Close is Friday. Q4 will land at 96.5% of plan. The CEO wants you to present the segment portfolio (BCG matrix) to investors on the Q4 call. A high-growth, low-share segment ('Embedded API') is dragging gross margin.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Investor call setup, headsets, slide on screen showing growth-share matrix

choices.label: Present the BCG honestly — Embedded API is a Question Mark; commit to a Q1 capital decision
choices.feedback: Analysts respected the honesty; the stock dipped 3% then recovered as the call went on.
choices.expert_rationale: Honest BCG framing on the analyst call (Embedded API as a Question Mark, with a Q1 capital-allocation answer ready) is what public-co-ready CFOs do. Analysts model you on transparency, not optimism.

choices.label: Roll up segments to one total; tell analysts 'we're investing in growth'
choices.feedback: Sell-side analyst pressed and you stumbled. Stock dropped 7% intraday.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Rolling segments into a single number is a yellow flag for any sell-side analyst. They'll model the worst case and price you accordingly.

choices.label: Announce an exit from the Embedded API segment on the call (premature)
choices.feedback: Customers panicked; ARR cut $2.4M overnight. Board wanted that decision in Q1, not on the call.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Announcing a segment exit on the call without a written board-approved plan creates a securities-law mess. Don't surprise the audit committee live.

score_bands.label: Public-co-ready CFO
score_bands.feedback: Owned misses, controlled close, kept the audit chair happy, and ran a clean covenant test. Vela could go public with you in the seat.

score_bands.label: Strong Series-D CFO run
score_bands.feedback: Solid quarter — tighten cash discipline and BCG segmentation rigor next time.

score_bands.label: Bumpy first close
score_bands.feedback: You got through it but the audit chair has questions and lender called.

score_bands.label: Re-run recommended
score_bands.feedback: Re-run focusing on owning misses early and not defending audit positions you can't win.

glossary_terms.definition: US revenue-recognition standard requiring identification of distinct performance obligations and allocation of contract price.
A condition in a loan or revolver — e.g. minimum cash, max leverage — whose breach triggers default or cure.
Window granted after a covenant breach to fix the issue before the lender takes formal action.
A weekly forward cash forecast — the operational tool that prevents covenant surprises.
Growth-share quadrant model — Star (high/high), Cash Cow (low/high), Question Mark (high/low), Dog (low/low).

coaching_moment.title: Reading the room before reading the spreadsheet
coaching_moment.body: A CFO who can't translate the numbers for a non-finance audience is a calculator, not a leader. Every quarter, the boardroom decides what story the numbers tell — and that story is what gets funded next year. Before you optimise a metric, ask: 'Who else needs to believe this?'

reflection_prompt: Which lever, if you'd moved it earlier, would have changed your outcome the most?
